title: The importance of diet

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The driving role of diet in the evolution of mammals has been clear for some time, according to Richard Wrangham, professor of biological anthropology at Harvard University. He is one of the leading researchers into the link between diet and changes in humans since we evolved away from the other primates, such as gorillas or chimpanzees. 'Dietary changes are well known to lead rapidly to changes in anatomy in other species,' says Wrangham. The first major dietary milestone in human evolution was a big increase in meat consumption, occurring about two million years ago. Before that, our primate ancestors lived on a predominantly vegetarian diet. The move to a diet based predominantly on meat introduced the evolutionary conditions for the arrival of modern humans. It was a crucial step, because it reduced the amount of energy needed to chew and digest large amounts of vegetation to gain the calories and protein we need, believes Professor Craig Stanford, an anthropologist at the University of Southern California.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: But surely a high-meat diet would have been bad news for our ancestors? 'An increase in meat eating would be predicted to shorten life by promoting chronic diseases,' Stanford says. But Stanford's team has found 'meat-adaptive genes' that evolved to counteract such negative effects, and these genes were so successful that humans actually lived longer. They enabled human evolution to exploit the positive aspects of meat, like a reduced stomach capacity needed to obtain the required calories, protein and other nutrients. While some vegetables and fruit also contain the required protein, they take longer to digest.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The other leap forward in human dietary evolution was the discovery of fire, and hence cooking. 'Cooking brings big benefits,' says Wrangham. 'The most important is it increases the amount of energy obtained from food. Another is that it makes food softer, hence quicker to eat.' Wrangham argues that humans could not extract sufficient protein and energy from a diet of largely raw meat, and therefore cooking must have become widespread quite early in the evolution of modern humans, perhaps over one million years ago. Other scientists say there is no firm evidence of significant use of cooking until recently in evolutionary terms, that is just under 100,000 years ago.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Whatever the timing, nobody disputes that learning how to control fire, plus the development of tools for preparing meat, had a dramatic effect on human evolution. 'Cooking was an essential part of our adaptation,' says anthropologist Professor Alison Brooks from George Washington University in the USA. 'Cooking makes lots of plant foods more easily digestible or less toxic, enables humans to survive after their teeth fall out, and reduces bacteria, insects and parasites that inhabit wild foods.'

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: According to C Loring Brace, an anthropologist at the University of Michigan, cooking triggered another change. 'Human tooth size remained unchanged from nearly two million years ago until just about 100,000 years ago. After this it began to reduce by one per cent every 2,000 years, which kept up until just over 10,000 years ago.' Brace invokes the 'neutral theory' to explain this. According to this theory, when extreme adaptations, such as large teeth for chewing raw meat, are no longer favoured by natural selection, they should revert back to their normal size.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: So how do changes in diet actually drive evolution of our genes? Some important clues have emerged following the recent discovery of a phenomenon called 'epigenetic inheritance'. Epigenetics tells us how our genes communicate with the surrounding environment. Every cell in our bodies contains the same DNA and therefore the same genes. But in order to develop the multitude of molecules we need for our various organs, tissues and immune systems, some of these genes become masked by chemical mechanisms during early development. This much has been known for a long time, but more recently it has become clear that some epigenetic changes can also be introduced through interactions between our genes and the environment, especially the food we eat. And a few of these changes can be passed on to our children in different ways.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Firstly, mothers can affect their unborn child by what they eat during pregnancy and later through breast-feeding. Secondly, there is evidence that parents can pass on epigenetic changes that have occurred as a result of what they eat, through their eggs and sperm. In the case of males, the critical time may be during their 'slow growth' period between the ages of nine and twelve. While this second link may be more speculative, there are a number of studies suggesting, strangely, that males with plenty to eat during their slow growth period are more likely to have children and even grandchildren who suffer from diabetes. The strongest evidence for this comes from examination of records from the isolated Swedish village of Överkalix in the 1800s, linking health to the success of the year's harvest. Analysis of the data carried out at the Institute of Child Health in London revealed that children whose fathers' slow growth period coincided with cool summers resulting in a poor harvest were more likely to be free of diabetes and less prone to heart disease. Therefore, what we eat might not only be important to ourselves and our children, but also to the evolution of the species.
